opus-5.5.text:
I think the big shift with AlphaZero was that it removed human knowledge from the equation almost entirely. AlphaGo was an incredible achievement, but it was bootstrapped from human expert games. We trained a policy network on a large dataset of professional Go games first, and only then did self-play reinforcement learning on top of that. It also had a fair amount of Go-specific engineering: handcrafted input features, rollout policies, and so on.

With AlphaZero, and with AlphaGo Zero before it, we asked a simple question: what if you start from completely random play and learn everything through self-play? No human games, no domain heuristics beyond the rules. What we found was that the system not only learned to play, it surpassed the version trained on human data, and fairly quickly. That was a surprise to a lot of people, including some of us. Human data turned out to be a crutch that limited the system somewhat. It anchored it to how humans think about the game.

The second part is generality. AlphaGo was a Go program. AlphaZero was one algorithm, with the same architecture and essentially the same hyperparameters, that mastered Go, chess, and shogi. Chess in particular had decades of very specialized engines with enormous amounts of human-tuned evaluation knowledge, and a general method that learned from scratch in hours was able to beat them. That told us we weren't just solving a game. We had a recipe: a neural network that guides search, and search that in turn produces better training targets for the network. That loop of planning and learning improving each other can scale.

So for me it was a game changer because it showed you could get superhuman performance from first principles, and that the same method transfers across domains. That's the idea that led directly to MuZero, where we even removed the need to know the rules, and I think it's still one of the most important lessons as we think about combining learning with search and reasoning in today's systems.

r001.rationale: It says AlphaZero started from random play, learned through self-play without human games, and achieved superhuman performance.

r002.rationale: It describes learning without human games and transfer across Go, chess, and shogi, but does not connect that independence to domains with insufficient human data.

r003.rationale: It does not mention AlphaGo robustness problems or say AlphaZero’s learning method resolved them.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that AlphaGo, for all the attention it got, was still in some sense a hand-built system. We had supervised learning on human expert games to bootstrap the policy, we had hand-crafted features going into the networks, we had a lot of Go-specific engineering. It beat Lee Sedol, which was extraordinary, but if you'd asked us to do the same thing for chess or shogi the next day, we would have had to start over with a different team of domain experts.

AlphaZero removed all of that. It starts from completely random play, it knows nothing except the rules of the game, and it learns entirely through self-play with search. The same algorithm, the same network architecture, the same hyperparameters more or less, and it reached superhuman level in Go, chess and shogi. That generality is the real change. It's not a Go program anymore, it's a learning method.

The other thing that struck me, and I think a lot of people felt this, is what it says about human knowledge. Centuries of accumulated opening theory in chess, in Go, and the system rediscovers a lot of it within hours, and then it also discards some of it and finds things we had never considered. That told us the human prior wasn't just unnecessary, in some cases it was actually a ceiling. Removing it let the system go further.

And from an engineering point of view it was simpler. One network outputting policy and value, Monte Carlo tree search as the improvement operator, and a very clean loop: search produces better targets than the raw network, the network trains towards them, and the improved network makes the search stronger. That loop is elegant, and it's the reason the ideas carried over so naturally to MuZero and beyond, where we stopped even assuming we knew the rules.

r001.rationale: It says AlphaZero starts from random play, learns through self-play, and reaches superhuman level across Go, chess, and shogi.

r002.rationale: It says AlphaZero does not rely on human training data and can transfer across games, but does not connect this to domains with insufficient human data.

r003.rationale: It contrasts AlphaZero’s learning method with AlphaGo’s hand-built components, but does not attribute the resolution of AlphaGo’s robustness problems to that method.

astra-6.text:
AlphaGo showed that we could build a system that could beat the best human players at Go, but it initially learned from human games. AlphaZero removed that dependency. We gave it the rules, and it learned entirely through self-play, starting without examples of how humans play.

That’s a significant shift because you’re no longer using human expertise as the starting point. The system can discover its own strategies. And the same approach worked across Go, chess, and shogi, which showed that it wasn’t just a solution tailored to one game. It was a more general way of learning to make decisions through experience.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaZero learned through self-play from the rules, but does not state that it achieved superhuman performance.

r002.rationale: It says the method worked across three games, but does not connect independence from human training data to domains with insufficient human data.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention AlphaGo’s robustness problems or say AlphaZero’s learning method resolved them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is that AlphaZero showed how much you could achieve without learning from human examples. With AlphaGo, we initially trained on games played by humans and then improved through self-play. AlphaZero started from the rules and learned entirely by playing against itself.

And the same approach worked across Go, chess, and shogi. That was exciting because it suggested we had found something more general than a technique for mastering one particular game. By combining learning with search, the system could discover strong strategies for itself, without us having to tell it what good play should look like.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaZero learned strong strategies from the rules through self-play, but does not state that it achieved superhuman performance.

r002.rationale: It links independence from human examples to generality across Go, chess, and shogi, but does not connect that independence to domains with insufficient human data.
